newsitem.title: USA: IMF panel chief backs big boost in Fund resources.
newsitem.headline: IMF panel chief backs big boost in Fund resources.

text.p: By Rich Miller, U.S. Economics Correspondent

The head of the IMF's powerful Interim Committee on Tuesday called for agreement next year on a major boost in IMF resources, warning that failure to do so could shake confidence in the lending agency.

"It is quite important that the Fund keep a high liquidity ratio to keep the confidence of all its members," Philippe Maystadt, chairman of the International Monetary Fund policy-making committee, told Reuters in an interview.

Maystadt, who is also Belgian Finance Minister, said the IMF's liquidity ratio -- which measures the amount of capital it has on hand against the call on its resources -- is likely to fall to its lowest level in nearly 15 years in 1997.

IMF resources have been drained by a series of big loans last year -- to Mexico and Russia in particular -- as the United States and its allies have increasingly turned to the Fund for help in keeping the world economy on an even keel.
IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus has proposed a doubling in the IMF's $220 billion capital to help cope with the added call on its resources.
"This truly will be a critical priority in the coming months," Camdessus told the opening plenary session of the IMF/World Bank annual meeting on Tuesday.
Maystadt described Camdessus's call for a doubling of Fund capital as an opening bid and doubted the increase would be that high.
But he said that all of the IMF's member nations, including the United States, agree that the Fund's capital needs to be boosted by at least 50 percent.
The money will not be available for at least two years after an agreement is reached, because of the need to have the pact ratified by national parliaments, he added.
Maystadt also said the Fund should know next year whether it will need to proceed with the controversial sale of some of its gold to finance stepped-up aid to poor nations.
Camdessus, backed by most of the IMF's member nations, has proposed selling up to five million ounces of the Fund's gold for that purpose.
But a handful of countries, led by Germany, have opposed gold sales, arguing that the IMF should instead depend on contributions from member nations for the needed financing.
Maystadt though suggested that Germany would go along with the gold sale should bilateral contributions from IMF member nations fall short of what is needed.
"There is an understanding agreed upon," he said. "If the need arises we must all be prepared to optimize the use of the Fund's reserves."
